messages.subject: Re: Error in data.frame(..., check.names = FALSE): arguments imply differing number of rows: 0, 1
messages.subject_clean: Error in data.frame(..., check.names = FALSE): arguments imply differing number of rows: 0, 1
messages.body_plain:
Hello.
There is a situation that is not commented on in any discussion forum about R and that presents this same error. It might help you. I also spent wasted days trying to solve this.
In my case, the columns with characters from my data.frame were not converted to factors. Therefore, the length of these columns was different from the other columns (numeric variables), generating this error commented on in this post. This prevented me from generating a graph (visreg package) with the results of my GLM. This is because in the latest version of R (4.0.0) the default stringsAsFactors (from the read.table function) have been changed from TRUE to FALSE.
So if this is the case for you, try the following:
read.table (file name, header = T, stringsAsFactors = T)
Hope this helps.
Bye.

messages.body_plain:
Hello unmarked folk,

I’m running a model within a Year-Stratified-N-Mixture-Model framework where I employed ‘pcount’ function of unmarked package.

I describe here the most parsimonious model's structure:

M = 3931 (grid cells 20*20 km)
response {Ci,j,t}: illegal offtake events (spanning over 9 years)

Model:
pcount(formula = ~ue + ug + rs ~ -1 + np + pa + nha + wr + el +
    rd + yr, data = umf, mixture = "NB", se = T, control = list(trace = T,
    REPORT = 5))

Three explanatory variables as linear effect for parameter ‘p’ :

1. unemployment metric (spanning over 9 years)
2. ranger post (constant)
3. mammals abundance (spanning across 9 years)

As for the abundance parameter ’N’, I regarded linear effects of protected areas categories (np + pa + nha + wr ) and excluded intercept and year effect (spanning over 9 years).

I tried to run goodness-of-fit test bootstrapping for that parsimonious model with nsim=2, 20, and 50 and 99, it works for all these ‘nsim’ choices, but when I ran 100, 200 or 500, I keep receiving the Error message below:

}
system.time(gof.NB <- parboot(fm23, fitstats, nsim =100, report = 1))
print(gof.NB) #  15:26 am 26 May 2020
str(gof.NB) #

#++++++++++++++Error++++++++++#

Error in checkForRemoteErrors(val) :
  3 nodes produced errors; first error: object 'yr' not found
In addition: There were 50 or more warnings (use warnings() to see the first 50)
Timing stopped at: 5.753 0.848 17.85

I appreciate if you could kindly provide me some advices to understand and solve this issue?

regards

Mahmood

messages.body_plain:
Dear all, I'm hoping to get some feedback on an approach I'm considering to assess model fit given my somewhat problematic dataset.

To give a background:

I'm using "unmarked" to model single-season (bird) occupancy at various survey locations that have employed both point counts and audio recording (ARUs). In the analysis I'm interested in what factors impact detection probabilities rather than occupancy. The ARUs have been repeatedly sampled within-day, as we are interested in temporal patterns in detection over the morning (I'm including a temporal auto-correlation term to deal with the proximity of the sampling in time). Due to the design, some sites have >20 repeated measures within season. I want to assess GOF and have been using the MacKenzie and Bailey goodness-of-fit test. The Chi-sq values for some species are mammoth and from my reading I gather that the MacKenzie-Bailey test does not perform well with datasets that have a high ratio of resampling to total survey sites because very rare detection histories become increasingly common and inflate the Chi-sq.  This seems to be what is happening with my output (note the >10,000,000 value):

My question is, can I work around this limitation by reducing the number of repeated measures for the GOF test only? Doing so would mean more cohorts were pooled together. I would use the full dataset for the final models. Right now I've tried this by limiting the data to a maximum of 10 repeated measures per site and this appears to improve the output substantially. messages.body_plain:
I've been working on a new package that might eventually help address this gap. It's meant to be a sort of middle ground between unmarked and BUGS. It has an interface nearly identical to unmarked, that uses Stan in the background to fit the models. The main advantages are that you can fit models with random effects (using lme4 syntax), get posterior distributions, and have access to all the cool cutting edge diagnostic stuff in rstan and related packages.

For example, you can fit a single-season occupancy model with a random effect on psi like this:

library(ubms)

umf <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y=y, siteCovs=dat_occ, obsCovs=dat_p)

ufit <- stan_occu(~x2~x1+ (1 | group), umf, chains=3)

which gives:

Call:
stan_occu(formula = ~x2 ~ x1 + (1 | group), data = umf, chains = 3)

(Intercept)        0.215 0.270 -0.327  0.740   979 1.01
x1                -0.499 0.114 -0.730 -0.283  3695 1.00
sigma [1|group]    1.241 0.253  0.825  1.819  1772 1.00

Detection:
            Estimate     SD  2.5% 97.5% n_eff  Rhat
(Intercept)    0.329 0.0619 0.206 0.447  4147 0.999
x2             0.532 0.0588 0.418 0.647  4514 1.000

LOOIC: 2310.822

While not as fast as unmarked, it can be pretty fast due to the efficient Stan sampler and because the likelihoods are marginalized. So far I've only implemented Stan versions of occu(), occuRN(), and pcount() but working to add more. If anyone wants to test or contribute, here's the github repo:

messages.subject: gdistsamp with Multi(!)-year Multi(!)-visit
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm analyzing a large dataset of drive counts of mountain gazelles, focusing on trends along a period of 16 years

The counts are done along a continuous 12 km transect. Alas only one short segment (500 m., one side) is appropriate for distance sampling analyses, due to restricted visibility.

Still, there are many observations from there, and when you look at the encounter rate (mean number of individuals observed per survey), this segment exhibits trends very similar to those observed when the entire transect is used.

The count is repeated 4 times a month, twice starting at sunset and twice 2 hours before sunset. I'm analyzing data for 2004-2019, a total of 712 surveys (some were missed along the years).

Each record holds the distance to the animal/s, sex and number of individuals, and off course comes with additional data on both the survey and observation levels – temp., wind-speed, rain, moon phase…

When conditions are less preferable, these animals will simply lie down in the shade, and become very hard to detect. In summer, for example, they shift to more nocturnal activity.

So, there are changes in their diel activity patterns , which vary between sexes, seasons and time of day (morning/evening). Animals may also simply lay down when it's too hot or too cold at a particular time.

>From what I read, I gather that gdistsamp is appropriate for this analysis, as it models the availability of animals for being observed, and I need some advice. I read previous discussions around multi-year multi-visits issues, but none was with such a large data set, and in any case, I want to make sure that I understand correctly.

So: does it make sense to stack all surveys in a year as one "transect", and then use a numPirmary of 48 visits to each (12 months X 4 times a month), with month, season, time of day, temperature (averaged over the 2 hours of survey), etc. as yearlySiteCovs?

Any comment on that and other insights will be highly appreciated.

Thanks,

Amir

Dear unmarked users,

I am new to this field.

I conducted anuran roadside calling survey in Taiwan by adapting the method from the North American Amphibian Monitoring Program (NAAMP).

The calling index (i.e. 0-3) was used  to represent the relative abundance of a specific anuran.

I would like to use "unmarked" package taking into accounts detection probability to assess the association between land use variables and anuran relative abundance.

Previous studies generally converted the calling index into a binary variable (i.e. presence/absence; 1/0); however, I think this measure may lead to loss of information.

In my study area, an anuran species had 100% occupancy rate. This species indeed significantly and positively associated with the area of agricultural land according to multivariate linear regression.

However, When I converted  the calling index to binary outcome and assessed the relationships between land use variables and this species by occupancy model (occu function) or multi-season occupancy model (colext), none of land use variables were associated with the occurrence. This is may due to the 100% occupancy rate of this species.

I am currently trying to use the N-mixture model (pcount function in unmarked) in this case and input the original values of calling index into the model. But I am not sure is it appropriate to use pcount function for calling index, a ordinal data? Or should I use the other functions?

Could unmarked package deal with the ordinal data?

I would greatly appreciate it if you could give me any suggestions. Thank you very much.

Chau-Ren

Hi Amir,

This seems reasonable to me, assuming you are OK with the assumption that variability in counts among replicates within a given year is due entirely to temporary emigration, and not also births, deaths, etc. If not you might want to stack the surveys in smaller groups (eg by month instead). Or you could try to handle both using a single model, but unmarked doesn't support that explicitly, so you'd have to use BUGS or similar software (discussed in sections 9.5.4.3 and 9.6 of Applied Hierarchical Modeling in Ecology).

Ken

plot2 <- function (x, y, panels = 1, colorkey, strip=FALSE,
    ylab="Site", xlab="Observation", ...)
{
    y <- getY(x)
    ym <- max(y, na.rm=TRUE)
    M <- nrow(y)
    J <- ncol(y)
    y <- as.data.frame(y)
    colnames(y) <- paste("obs",1:J)
    y$site <- 1:M
    sites.per.panel <- M/panels
    y$group <- as.factor(round(seq(1,panels,length=M)))
    y2 <- reshape(y, idvar=c("site", "group"), varying=list(1:ncol(getY(x))),
              v.names="value", direction="long")
    y2$variable <- factor(paste("obs", y2$time), levels=colnames(y))
    if(missing(colorkey))
        colorkey <- list(at=0:(ym+1), labels=list(labels=as.character(0:ym),
            at=(0:ym)+0.5))
    levelplot(value ~ variable*site | group, y2,
        scales=list(relation="free", x=list(labels=1:J)),
        colorkey=colorkey, strip=strip, xlab=xlab, ylab=ylab,...)
}

Hi there! I’m having issues with the predict function in unmarked. With my point count data (3 visits to 26 sites), I’m using the same code and model set to select top abundance models for the species I most frequently observed (n>37 for each). While I’ve gotten reasonable predictions for most species (between 0 and 6), I’ve gotten absurdly large predictions for others (see reduced code/output below for example). My models seem to fit the data well regardless of species… any clue what’s happening here?  Thanks in advance for your help and input!

library(unmarked)

birdabun.data <- read.csv("~/Unmarked/pcountformatdata.csv",row.names=1)

birdabun.y <- birdabun.data[,c("INBU1", "INBU2", "INBU3")]

#-------- Load/Standardize variables ------------

#canopy cover

cancov.mean <- mean(birdabun.data$canopy_cover)

cancov.sd <http://cancov.sd> <- sd(birdabun.data$canopy_cover)

cancov.z <- (birdabun.data$canopy_cover-cancov.mean)/cancov.sd <http://cancov.sd>

#TREATMENT: i = invaded; r=removed

treat <-  as.factor(birdabun.data$treatment)

#--------- Create unmarkedFrame -------------

birdabun.umf <- unmarkedFramePCount(

    y=birdabun.y,

    siteCovs=data.frame(cancov=cancov.z, treat=treat),

    obsCovs=list(time=birdabun.data[,c("time_1", "time_2", "time_3")],

                 noise=birdabun.data[,c("noise_1", "noise_2", "noise_3")],

                 date=birdabun.data[,c("date_1", "date_2", "date_3")]))

obsCovs(birdabun.umf) <- scale(obsCovs(birdabun.umf))

#---------- Model selection ---------------------

#top models - both models have good fit

(P12    <- pcount(~ date+ time + noise   ~ treat, birdabun.umf))

messages.subject_clean: Population level confidence intervals without parboot
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I’m using gdistsamp to estimate abundance. I've used predict to get abundance estimates for a large number of fine scale pixels. I've taken the estimate of the total population size to be the sum of the predicted value for all pixels and I'm now trying to calculate a confidence interval for this value. I've tried to use parboot for this but due to the large number of pixels it’s going to take weeks to run.

Is there a way I can calculate a confidence interval manually or will I need to increase my pixel size (i.e. reduce the number of pixels) until parboot will run in a reasonable timeframe?

We’re concerned that simply adding up the lower and upper predicted values for all pixels might unduly inflate the CIs because it assumes positive covariance among pixels. We’d like to use something like the delta method, assuming there is no covariance among pixels.

I’ve tried taking the square root of the sum of the squared SEs for all pixels, multiplying by 1.96 and adding to/subtracting from the total population estimate to get a 95% CI. I did this on the log scale since that’s what the model uses for abundance, but I end up with “Inf” when I try to back transform the resulting values so clearly that’s not quite right.

Any advice would be much appreciated.

Many thanks,

Zoe

messages.body_plain:
Hi Zoe,

You could use the delta method. Just to re-use some dummy code posted elsewhere, to get an estimate of Var(N-hat), you could try something like:

library(emdbook)
Var_hat<-deltavar(sum(exp(b0+b1*Forest)),
                         meanval=c(b0=estimateb0, b1=estimateb1),
                          Sigma=[variance and covariance for b0, b1])
SE<-sqrt(Var_hat)

Above, assume 'Forest' is a pixel level covariate, so a vector of length nPixels--you'd have to change the beta arguments, lengths, etc. as needed. The variance covariance matrix can be grabbed from the fitted model.

There are a couple of options for constructing the CI. Maybe a lognormal approach makes the most sense. Something like dropping the exp in the deltavar call, and exponentiating log[LCI, UCI]--should be able find some formal descriptions around.

I guess you could also use monte carlo simulation based on the predicted pixel values and estimated variance, although I don't know that there would be any substantive advantage to doing so.

The approaches above focus on expected abundance (a lambda_i rather than the latent N_i), but if you've only sampled a small number of the cells you are trying to predict across, the difference in the CI shouldn't be substantial.

John
